facts.fact: Asian arowana (Scleropages formosus) reaches about 900 mm standard length.
Silver and black arowana reach about 90 cm in aquaria; wild silvers reach 120 cm.
Asian arowana has been on CITES Appendix I since 1975; legal fish come from registered CITES breeders and should be microchipped with official papers.
Asian arowana trade is illegal in some countries, such as the United States.
Arowanas are solitary and usually best kept alone; any tankmates must be large, bottom-dwelling fish.
Arowana lifespan is 10–20+ years with proper care.
Juvenile South American arowanas are easy to keep, but adults are extremely hard to keep.
PetMD gives a minimum tank of 150+ gallons depending on species, but its FAQ says adults need at least 250 gallons.
Tank footprint matters more than height.
Asian arowana needs a tank at least 2 m long and suits only public or the very largest private aquaria.
Some sources suggest 240 x 90 x 90 cm for one adult silver arowana; the author notes not everyone agrees.
Temperature 72–82 F, changing no more than ±2 F per day; pH 6.0–7.0; nitrite as close to zero as possible.
Asian arowana: 22–28°C, pH 5.0–8.0, hardness 2–15 dGH.
Silver and black arowana: pH 5.8–7.0, hardness under 14–15°dH, 24–30°C.
Freshwater salt is optional; if used, keep specific gravity at 1.004 and change it by no more than ±0.001 in 24 hours.
The filter should turn over the full tank volume at least 4 times per hour, for example at least 600 GPH for a 150-gallon tank.
Asian arowana needs high dissolved oxygen, so use external filters, powerheads or airstones.
Seriously Fish calls weekly 30–50% water changes mandatory for Asian arowana.
PetMD suggests 10–25% water changes every 2–4 weeks.
Arowanas produce a lot of waste, so frequent water changes and siphoning are essential.
Fit a tight hood: arowanas jump when startled.
Light the room gradually before switching on tank lights, to reduce sudden jumping.
Place the tank away from windows, direct sunlight and air conditioners.
Feed adults once daily and young fish two to three times daily; each meal should be finished within 1–2 minutes.
Thaw frozen food before feeding, and avoid hard-shelled insects or invertebrates for young fish.
Feed young Asian arowanas bloodworm, small earthworms and chopped prawn.
Feed adult Asian arowanas fish strips, whole prawns, mussels, live river shrimp, larger earthworms and pellets; pellets should not be the staple.
Offer floating food or feed at the surface, in small amounts.
Adult silver arowanas can take crickets, locusts, earthworms, prawns, mussels, cockles and fish chunks.
Feed with long tongs or a feeding stick, not fingers, which the fish may take for food.
Do not feed mammal or bird meat (beef heart, chicken): the fish may not metabolise some of the lipids, causing fat deposits and organ degeneration.
Livebearers and small goldfish as feeders carry parasite and disease risks and are not nutritious unless conditioned first.
Do not add Asian arowana to a biologically immature tank.
Do not replace all the water at once; it removes beneficial bacteria.
Do not buy juvenile arowanas that still have a yolk sac, as they are not yet feeding.
Common arowana illnesses: fin or tail rot, dropsy, parasites, bacterial infections, cancer, ich, pop eye, fungal infections and swim bladder disorders.
Warning signs: color change, lethargy, abnormal swimming, receding fins, not eating for over a day, flashing, rapid breathing, white spots, cloudy or bulging eyes, raised scales and bloating.
In drop eye, one or both eyes point permanently downward and may not return to normal.
Drop eye rarely resolves on its own and can worsen over time.
A keeper reports drop eye is most common in silver, jardini and leichardti arowanas, often after about 16–18", and rare in Asian arowanas except above 24".
Practical Fishkeeping links drop eye to feeding from the bottom, keeping bottom-dwelling tankmates and feeding live fish.
Jay Hemdal thinks mechanical trauma from hitting tank walls or lids is the main cause of drop eye, with clear-sided tanks contributing.
Hemdal notes fat buildup behind the eyes remains a possible cause, based on a British aquarium's necropsies.
Other proposed causes of drop eye include poor nutrition, inbreeding, stress, too much light and mycobacteriosis.
A Nha Trang practitioner blames eye displacement on wrong tank lighting, saying fish turn away from the light until their eyes shift.
Keepers report fish lice and anchor worms come mostly from live feeder foods.
Keepers report raised scales in young arowanas come from extreme temperature changes and dirty water.
Keepers report tilted gill covers come from fouled water (ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, low oxygen), cramped space and large temperature swings.
Hemdal suggests matching tank size to fish size and reducing collisions; drop eye is rarely seen in ponds.
Keep Asian arowana water stable and mature.
No proven treatment for drop eye exists; breeders move fish to outdoor ponds, and surgery has been reported.
A keeper's early treatment for cloudy eye: change 1/3 of the water, add salt and raise the temperature to 30-33°C, then change 1/4 every third day; recovery may take 3-5 months.
A keeper's treatment for raised scales: salt, 32-34°C, more aeration, a 1/4 water change every 3-4 days, plus copper sulfate (no dose given).
A keeper's treatment for ich and gill rot: 1% salt with 0.8 g quinine per liter, a 2-3°C temperature rise and more aeration, then disinfect the tank after recovery.
Keepers treat fish lice and anchor worms with copper sulfate (no dose given), and fish lice also with a concentrated salt soak plus extra oxygen.
For early tilted gill covers, keepers do an immediate 20% water change, repeated every 2-3 days, add aeration and put coral sand in the filter; hardened covers need surgical trimming.
If gill covers start curling, change 20% of the water at once and increase aeration.
Hemdal questions the claim that floating ping-pong balls cure drop eye; MFK keepers also say they do not fix it.
A keeper argues drop eye is not a disease because it cannot spread.
Hemdal doubts inbreeding causes drop eye, since wild-caught fish also get it.
Asian arowana is native to the Mekong system in Vietnam and Cambodia, but has been wiped out across much of its range.
Vietnamese names: Ngân Long (silver), Kim Long (gold), Thanh Long (green/blue) and Huyết Long (red); premium types include Quá bối.
Vietnamese keepers fear sudden temperature changes: in winter they cover the tank and use a heater, in summer a stainless steel mesh cover.
In Vietnam, adult arowanas are fed trạch (loach) twice a day, and young fish small river shrimp torn into pieces.
Vietnamese keepers say fungal infections and raised scales (xù vẩy) are common.
Fish are microchipped at 4–5 months (12–15 cm); the chip shows the farm of origin.
Many Vietnamese keepers import arowanas from Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
Arowanas are sized by length from whisker to tail in cm, and are commonly kept with cá sam and cá hổ.
In 2012, food and electricity cost about 1–2 million VND per month, more in winter.
A Nha Trang hobbyist surgically corrects drooping eyes under anesthesia in about 10 minutes, for 500,000–800,000 VND; recovery is in shallow tanks with salt and constant aeration.
Fungus on the barbels (nấm râu) is described as owners' biggest fear.
Kim Long takes about 1–2 years to turn gold, and Huyết Long 2–3 years to turn red, depending on diet, light, water and genetics.
Asian arowana color forms include green, super red, crossback golden and red tail golden.
